item.title: Life Is Mostly Annoying Little Things
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

Life Is Mostly Annoying Little Things

Consider the Russian word for the stuff that eats up your life.

Posted September 1, 2026

Natasha Kamneva
Source: Used with permission/Natasha Kamneva

You know all those little repetitive tasks you do day in and day out? The Russians, I found out, have a word for those: byt.

Byt refers to the daily business that keeps a life going. Brushing your teeth. Washing the dishes. Making the bed. Figuring out why your internet is slow. Calling Spectrum to get it fixed, waiting on hold, getting cut off, calling back. All the annoying little stuff.

I learned the word byt on my podcast Fifty Words For Snow, where my cohost Emily John Garces and I search for words from other languages without direct English equivalents. Last week, Emily and I spoke with Natasha Kamneva, a native Russian speaker from Moscow, about this word byt. Natasha explained that the word carries more weight than our term “daily life.” It refers to the accumulation of ordinary obligations that can crush our spirit.

The Russian poet Vladimir Mayakovsky famously wrote in his suicide note that “the love boat crashed into the byt,” meaning his joy and love of life crashed into the everyday business of living. The phrase has become proverbial in Russia to express how romance can be killed by practicalities.

This Wasn't Supposed to Happen

I tend to the look at the byt as an interference to my “real life,” the one I am supposed to be living if I could just get through all the dumb little tasks on my list. My real life, I feel, involves creativity and connection; laughter and love. It is my writing, my performing; my connection with friends and family. It does not involve figuring out why the garbage disposal is jammed, cleaning up where my dog has vomited, or trying to get the plumber to reduce his eight-hour-window so I can go out and get groceries again.

My response to byt is often some version of: Why is this happening to me? Not fair!

I’m starting to realize, however, that the problem isn’t the byt itself. It’s my expectation that life should contain a minimum of it, that a good life runs along smoothly with little tedium and no interference.

Expect the Half-Eaten Yam

For the podcast, we asked our reporter, Eric Giancoli, to record one ordinary day of byt. His report included back stretches, brushing his teeth, taking medicine, packing lunch, calling his sister about insurance for their mother, driving home, making dinner, and doing the dishes.

The dramatic low point was discovering that he had eaten the other half of his yam the night before and therefore had no starch for lunch. He called this “a shocking and brutal truth.” Then he had to scramble for another form of starch, a scramble he had not planned for. Something had gone wrong.

What if, I’ve been thinking, I began looking at the byt not as an interference to my real life, but as the essence of it? I’m starting to see that soaring creativity, artistic triumph, touching reunions, moving concerts, and heartfelt connection with friends do happen, and thank God they do. But they are not the main stuff of life. The main stuff is smaller and far less memorable: making dinner, picking up prescriptions, answering emails, putting gas in the car, looking for the charger, finding the charger, losing the charger, then looking for it again.

I have spent a lot of my life thinking of these things as what I have to get through in order to get back to my real life. I’m beginning to understand that they are my real life. Nothing has gone off course. Nothing has gone wrong. This is what a life looks like up close. The concert ends. Then you have to remember where you put that little ticket and find where you parked.

My new slogan is “Expect the byt.” Because even the love boat needs somebody to take out the trash.

item.title: Relationships as Assisting Forces
item.description:
Relationships

Relationships as Assisting Forces

How partners can become allies, not competitors.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • A partnership can provide attention, acceptance, appreciation, affection, and allowing.
  • A relationship can be an experience of alliance, not competition.
  • When misattunement occurs, partners can communicate feelings without blame and see attunement as learnable.

A healthy and trustworthy partner is an accompanying ally. Here are some specific ways one can become such an ally.

Attunement

An ally is someone who attunes to us in an empathic way. In an authentic intimate relationship, this moves in both directions. Attunement is deeply grasping what someone is saying and feeling. Empathic attunement means feeling what someone else feels. It means, in effect, mirroring or reflecting the other’s feeling by feeling it too and affirming it, by word, action, or gesture, that we understand it. We do this by showing the five A's: attention, appreciation, affection, acceptance, and allowing.

  • We pay attention to someone’s words, needs, feelings, and longings at a feeling level.
  • We appreciate and value someone’s feelings, which means we treat them with respect and don't try to talk them out of their feelings.
  • We hold and stay with the other’s concern or pain with physical affection that's appropriate to the nature of the connection.
  • We accept rather than reject the other person, making no attempts to change the other in accord with our likes, demands, or expectations.
  • We allow someone to be exactly who that someone is, rather than trying to be in control of his, her, or their behavior or choices. We are thereby doing what all allies do: honoring the other person’s deepest needs, values, and wishes.

Regarding acceptance, we may want love to be equal, in quality and quantity, between ourselves and our partner. Sometimes we even demand it or feel unloved if it is not happening. The mature question in a relationship is not about equivalence. It is about whether we can accept others’ limits and their different ways of showing love compared to our own. Maturity means saying: “I want to accept your brand of love, even though it is not the same as mine.”

With regard to allowing, our definition of control changes when we reach spiritual maturity. It is no longer in ego language; for example, “I am in charge here.” It is in sane, adult language; for example, “I can handle what happens.” We then step up to the plate and are ready to hear what an experience has to teach us. We follow with whatever action gets us through the situation. This is the healthy version of being in control.

When Misattunements Happen

Misattunements happen in all relationships. In an atmosphere of mended failures, the only atmosphere in which love can thrive, we see misattunement to our feelings not as a reason to blame the other. Instead, we tell the other what feeling or message of ours he or she missed. We do this in a non-blaming way:

“When I feel misattuned to you, I am glad to explain again what I feel.”

Or, “When I misattune to you, I ask that you let me know so I can try again.”

This helps us come to see attuning as a skill that any of us can learn. It is the skill of an assisting force. Also, when we fail to attune to a partner’s feeling, we might say: “I am not ashamed about this misattunement, though I am sorry about it. I am learning the skill of attuning and will keep practicing. I do not offer perfection, only the sincerity of my ongoing intention and efforts, however inadequate or tardy.”

If the assessment we are making about the other is irrational, we use a different protocol when asking for attunement: We ask for a partner’s presence while we do our own work, rather than ask to be rescued. Consider, for instance, if we suffer from insane jealousy and feel scared, even panicked, when our spouse has friendly contact with her ex-husband. She tells us there is no attraction left, no erotic component in her relationship to him. We know this is true, but we still feel fear. We know this irrational jealousy is a common pattern for us and that freedom from it is our personal work. So, we admit we are overreacting and ask her to hear about the paranoid shape our fear has taken. We also bravely ask her not to keep reassuring us that she is no longer attracted to him. That only coddles our fear and does not help us get over it. A true relationship/ally does not do that; she helps us face our fear, talk about it, feel it, but does not try to cancel it for us.

This is how an ally acts in an adult way and thereby helps us to be adult. In this situation, adult means letting go of jealousy that is not appropriate and letting go of the fear that is interfering with healthy relating. In our dialogue, our work is to admit our fear, to acknowledge it as irrational, and to show it verbally and bodily in a way that is appropriate. All our ally/partner has to do, and all we ask her to do, is listen. She is attuning to how we are triggered, but not jumping in to rescue us. She is thereby helping us move through it. Repeating this dialogue whenever we feel our irrational fear is the state-of-the-art adult way of releasing ourselves from it.

“Let me feel bad about this!” —Tim Hutton, in the film Ordinary People, asking his psychiatrist not to try to soothe him, only to stay with him as he experiences his suffering.

Adapted from my book By Your Side: How to Find Soulful Allies and Become One to Others (Shambhala, 2024).

item.title: Why Do Narcissists Need Narcissistic Supply From People?
item.description:
Narcissism

Why Do Narcissists Need Narcissistic Supply From People?

Narcissists, like children, need adults to reassure them of their value.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissists are like young children in that they over-rely on other adults for validation and support.
  • Heinz Kohut's treatment for NPD focuses on helping narcissists mature and need less external validation.
  • The object relations treatment for NPD focuses more on attaining whole object relations than on self-objects.
Source: Rawpixel / Pexels

All humans are born helpless. We depend on our caregivers for everything from soothing us to feeding us to making sure we are safe. If we are not taken care of by other humans, we die.

As we develop during childhood and our teens, we gradually start to take over the functions that our caregivers do for us. Eventually, if we are healthy, we learn how to dress ourselves, tell time, read, learn right from wrong, make friends, and so on. We learn to soothe ourselves through internalizing our experiences of being soothed.

What About Our Self-Image?

Charles Horton Cooley (1864–1929), a noted sociologist, introduced the concept of “The Looking Glass Self.” He theorized that one of the ways we form a sense of who we are is by internalizing the reactions that we believe other people have towards us. Other people act like a mirror in which we can see ourselves (1902).

Heinz Kohut (1913–1981), the brilliant Austrian American psychiatrist who revolutionized the treatment of narcissistic personality disorder, introduced the term “self-object” to describe how humans use other people as extensions of themselves to manage internal and external problems. If we look at children, we can see that they use their caregivers as self-objects (1971, 1977).

Kohut’s work gave birth to modern Self Psychology, one of the two main treatments for NPD. (The other is Object Relations).

Even when children are able to physically take care of themselves, they often still rely on their caregivers to soothe them, tell them everything will be okay, and reassure them that they are competent and lovable.

Kohut believed that our need for self-objects never entirely goes away. He concluded it is quite normal for most of us to continue to use other people to perform certain functions for us. However, if we needed to, we could and would perform them for ourselves.

Unlike the Object Relations approach to diagnosing NPD, which measures a narcissist’s progress in therapy by their attainment of whole object relations (the ability to see oneself and others in a realistic, integrated, and stable nuanced way that is not either all-good or all-bad), Self Psychology looks at the client’s reliance on self-objects and how much clients are capable of doing for themselves (Masterson, 1981). One of Kohut’s measures of whether therapy is helping a client with NPD is to look at whether that client is gradually taking over more functions and relying on self-objects less.

Our use of self-objects matures as we mature. We still could use an occasional hug, some praise, some protection, and some reassurance. However, this is optional and mentally healthy adults will not fall apart without this type of external support.

How Does This Relate to Narcissists?

People with narcissistic personality disorders are like young children with regard to their continued need for eternal validation. Even very high functioning and successful people with NPD still rely on other people to validate them.

If you are a narcissist, you can be the head of a giant company, a famous musician, universally admired as beautiful and talented, and still be quite childlike when it comes to your ability to soothe yourself, feel competent at your job, and manage your emotional ups and downs.

Narcissists still have a “Looking Glass Self.” Or, in Kohut’s terms, they need other people to act as self-objects to keep functioning well.

Note: I am using the terms narcissist, narcissistic, and NPD to describe people who qualify for a full diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder.

What Is Human Narcissistic Supply?

Very simply, human narcissistic supply consists of people who the narcissist relies on to help manage their self-esteem.

If you are in a relationship with someone with NPD, they will be using you as a self-object and a mirror. There are many different ways narcissists use people to help manage their self-esteem.

Here are the three most common narcissistic subtypes and how they use other people as self-objects to get narcissistic supply. In parentheses are some other common names for this subtype.

Exhibitionist NPD (Overt)

They directly and fairly obviously seek admiration, attention, and status. They want to be in the spotlight. They also love giving advice and telling long stories that they believe show them in a good light. They devalue, ignore, or are condescending to people they see as below them in the status hierarchy.

Closet NPD (Covert and Vulnerable)

They are afraid of looking foolish or being exposed as a fake. This makes them afraid of the spotlight and directly confronting people. Many do not fit people’s picture of NPD because they appear to lack confidence and seek reassurance and the approval of people above them in whatever status hierarchy they value. They attach themselves to people, religions, clothes, books, and objects that they can brag about.

They are too insecure to directly ask for your admiration. Instead, they seek your admiration for whomever and whatever they are currently using as a self-object. They may tell you that their religion is the best, their mate is the smartest person alive, and you should watch their favorite television show.

Now, anybody might tell you this, but if they are closet narcissists, it really, really matters to them that you agree with their assessments. The average non-narcissistic person who tells you this is just trying to share things that they think you might enjoy or find useful. It does not really matter to them if you take their advice. You can say that you don’t enjoy the music they suggested, and they will not pick a fight with you over it.

Malignant Narcissist (Toxic, Devaluing, Sadistic; Can Be Overt or Covert)

Malignant narcissists get their narcissistic supply from destroying the self-esteem and happiness of other people. If you are their partner, you are the one they are destroying to get narcissistic supply. They feel better and smarter and stronger when they hurt you.

Summary

We all occasionally use other people to perform functions for us—cheer us up, reassure us that our outfit looks good, and applaud our successes. However, narcissists take this to another level. They are almost entirely dependent on the people around them to validate their self-worth.
